units.text: 15. Are there things even intelligence cannot compute?

‘If we knew all the laws, we could predict everything.’ This sentence compresses at least three assumptions: that we also knew the relevant state, that we could perform the computation and that the question had a solution accessible through a general method. None comes free with the list of equations.

The first limit is observational. We measure with a certain precision and do not control every condition. In a sensitive system, very small initial differences can grow over time until detailed predictions diverge. Lorenz’s model shows how simple deterministic equations can produce nonperiodic evolutions sensitive to initial state. Determinism is not equivalent to practical predictability (Lorenz, 1963) .

This does not mean we can say nothing. Some statistical properties or outcome ranges may be predictable even when the exact trajectory is not. Moving from ‘I do not know the detail’ to ‘everything is equally probable’ is an error. The prediction limit must be formulated at the level of the question and time horizon.

The second limit concerns resources. A computation possible in principle may require too much time, memory or energy for a concrete observer. Seth Lloyd’s research on physical limits to computation links computational capacity to resources and physical theory. These are not proofs about every metaphysically possible substrate; they are limits formulated within specified physical frameworks (Lloyd, 2000) .

The third limit is more severe: absence of a general algorithm for a precise problem class. Cubitt, Pérez-García and Wolf proved undecidability of the spectral-gap problem for certain families of quantum lattice systems in the thermodynamic limit. This does not mean every finite material has a property impossible to investigate. It means the desired universal procedure solving every instance of the constructed class does not exist (Cubitt, Pérez-García și Wolf, 2022) .

It is tempting to use such theorems as a general certificate of mystery. That would be a mistake. An undecidability proof has a domain and premises. It does not tell us the particular problem on our desk is insoluble, that intuition solves it miraculously or that science has reached its end. It forces us to relinquish a universal promise, not the investigation of cases.

Nor do Gödel’s theorems authorize ‘every important truth exceeds reason’. They concern limits of formal systems with precise properties. Leaping from arithmetic to claims about soul, cosmos or an AI’s omniscience requires additional arguments. Invoking a mathematical name is not one of them (Raatikainen, 2025) .

There is another limit, often more relevant than computational difficulty: identifiability. Can two different mechanisms produce exactly the same available observations? If so, an observer cannot separate them merely by analyzing the same data more carefully. This is not lack of intelligence but lack of a difference in accessible information.

An elementary example: a thermometer displays 20, and we do not know whether the temperature is 20 and the instrument correct, or the temperature is 18 and the instrument has a constant two-unit error. More identical records do not resolve the ambiguity. An independent standard or another intervention type may resolve it. The problem requires not merely more computation, but different information.

In the simulation hypothesis, this distinction becomes decisive. A simulated and a nonsimulated world might have the same results for every permitted internal experiment. In that case, lack of evidence would not necessarily stem from a simulator’s conspiracy. It would stem from observational equivalence of the descriptions.

There is also selection among the questions we can formulate. An observer built from a world’s processes can access only certain variables. But we should not turn this observation into a grand paradox before describing a model. We can prove limits in a well-defined formal system; we cannot assume every imagined limit applies to our universe.

Being rigorous about limits paradoxically means being more ambitious. Instead of saying ‘it cannot be understood’, we ask: can it not be measured, not be computed with available resources, does no general algorithm exist, or is there no observable difference? Each diagnosis suggests a different research program. Confusing them produces needless resignation and impossible promises.
